title: Benchmark
text:
This benchmark uses NGC1512_cube_mockGCs.fits, a mixed cube containing extended galaxy structure, compact GC-like sources, and sky contamination in the same field. It is designed to answer two practical questions:

How much reconstruction quality is lost relative to PCA?
Does the mixed smooth+sparse spatial prior produce more concentrated compact components than vanilla NMF?


The benchmark uses outer-spaxel sky subtraction, weighted spatial smoothing for extended components, and sparse priors for the designated compact components.

mean_top1pct and mean_top5pct measure how much component-weight mass is carried by the brightest 1% or 5% of map pixels. Higher values indicate more concentrated maps. For the designated sparse components, the sparse_top1pct and sparse_top5pct columns isolate that concentration test.

title: Benchmark
text:
How To Read The Figure

The reconstruction panel checks whether the mixed prior preserves acceptable spaxel-level fits.
The white-light panel is the key visual check: if the model is isolating GC-like sources, the sparse-component peaks should land on visually compact knots in the asinh image.
The sparse-component maps panel is the main spatial diagnostic for whether the sparse prior is isolating localized structure.
The residual-energy panel is secondary: PCA is expected to win on pure rank-(k) squared-error reconstruction.



In the current saved run, spatial NMF improves the vanilla NMF reconstruction MSE from 0.000399 to 0.000322, while increasing the designated sparse-component top-1% concentration from 0.057 to 0.113.


Even in the saved run above, the sparse components should be read cautiously: the current model improves concentration metrics relative to vanilla NMF, but the candidate peaks still collapse onto the bright central galaxy light rather than separating visually distinct GC-like sources. At this stage the benchmark is a useful failure case, not a polished detection result.

title: Benchmark
text:
Recommended Settings
The current benchmark run uses:

k = 8
outer-spaxel sky subtraction
lambda_smooth for spectral regularization
Gaussian spatial coupling for smooth components
sparse priors on the compact-source components

title: Benchmark
text:
Interpretation
PCA remains the strongest baseline for pure rank-(k) squared-error reconstruction, so the main question is not whether NMF beats PCA on MSE alone. The relevant question is whether spatial NMF preserves acceptable reconstruction quality while yielding cleaner and more interpretable component-weight maps. On the current NGC1512 run, the answer is only partial: the mixed prior improves concentration and reconstruction relative to vanilla NMF, but it does not yet produce a convincing GC-isolation result.

title: SpaxNMF
text:
Spatially aware NMF for integral-field spectroscopy




SpaxNMF fits non-negative component spectra together with component-weight maps, combining smooth spectral regularization, Gaussian spatial coupling, and optional sparse priors for compact sources.


Get Started See the Benchmark







Shared non-negative component spectra recovered from the full cube.


Gaussian spatial coupling on component-weight maps for extended structure.


Optional sparse priors for compact-source components such as GC-like signals.


Real-cube diagnostics against PCA and vanilla NMF under matched preprocessing.



The full objective, kernel weighting, and optimization details are documented on the Model page.

title: SpaxNMF
text:
Core Factorization



Factorization


Shared spectra, spatially varying weights

\[
X \approx AS
\]

X is the spaxel-by-wavelength matrix, A is the component-weight matrix, and S contains the component spectra.




Spatial term


Weighted coherence between neighboring spaxels

\[
w_{ij} = \exp\left(-\frac{d_{ij}^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)
\]

This term discourages noisy salt-and-pepper maps by penalizing strong changes between nearby component weights while allowing distant spaxels to decouple.

title: SpaxNMF
text:
Real-Cube Benchmark



NGC1512 galaxy + compact sources + sky


The current benchmark uses NGC1512_cube_mockGCs.fits, a mixed IFU cube containing extended galaxy structure, compact GC-like sources, and sky contamination in the same field. The comparison applies the same outer-spaxel sky subtraction and matched preprocessing before fitting PCA, vanilla NMF, and the mixed spatial+sparse model.



<p class='benchmark-inline'>On the saved NGC1512 benchmark, the mixed spatial+sparse fit reduces the vanilla NMF MSE from 0.000399 to 0.000322 while raising the designated compact-component top-1% concentration from 0.057 to 0.113.</p>



Use the benchmark page for the full figure, saved metrics, and the exact run configuration used to generate them.


Open the real-cube benchmark




What the benchmark is for


This benchmark is intended as a technical validation target rather than a front-page showcase. It is useful for checking whether the mixed spatial+sparse prior improves compact-component concentration and preserves acceptable reconstruction quality under matched preprocessing.



PCA remains the rank-(k) squared-error baseline.


Vanilla NMF provides the non-negative comparison without spatial coupling.


SpaxNMF adds Gaussian spatial smoothing and optional sparse compact-source components.


The full figure, saved metrics, and run settings live on the benchmark page.



Use the benchmark page when you want the detailed diagnostic, not the main landing-page overview.

title: Model
text:
SpaxNMF represents an IFU cube as a matrix (X _{}^{n p}), with one row per spaxel and one column per wavelength channel. The model seeks a low-rank non-negative factorization
\[
X \approx AS
\]
where:

(A _{}^{n k}) contains component weights for each spaxel
(S _{}^{k p}) contains the component spectra
(k) is the chosen factorization rank

A should be interpreted simply as a set of component-weight maps over the field.

title: Model
text:
SpaxNMF represents an IFU cube as a matrix (X _{}^{n p}), with one row per spaxel and one column per wavelength channel. The model seeks a low-rank non-negative factorization
\[
X \approx AS
\]
where:

(A _{}^{n k}) contains component weights for each spaxel
(S _{}^{k p}) contains the component spectra
(k) is the chosen factorization rank

A should be interpreted simply as a set of component-weight maps over the field.

title: Model
text:
Objective Function
The current implementation minimizes
\[
\mathcal{L}(A,S)=
\|X-AS\|_F^2
+\lambda_S \|DS\|_F^2
+\sum_c \lambda_{A,c}\sum_{i,j} w_{ij}(A_{ic}-A_{jc})^2
+\sum_c \lambda_{C,c}\|A_{:,c}\|_1
\]
with Gaussian spatial couplings
\[
w_{ij} = \exp\left(-\frac{d_{ij}^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).
\]



Reconstruction term


(|X-AS|_F^2) matches the model to the observed spectra.




Spectral smoothness


(_S |DS|_F^2) penalizes channel-to-channel roughness in the recovered component spectra.




Spatial coherence


(_{A,c}) controls how strongly nearby spaxels are encouraged to carry similar weights for component (c).

title: Model
text:
Why The Spatial Term Matters
The spatial regularization does not smooth the spectra directly. It acts on the component weights in (A):
\[
\sum_{i,j} w_{ij}(A_{ic}-A_{jc})^2
\]
for each selected component (c). In practice this:

suppresses salt-and-pepper weight maps
stabilizes the decomposition under noise
encourages extended components to remain spatially coherent
leaves distant spaxels free to differ because the kernel weight decays with distance

title: Model
text:
Compact-Source Components
Selected components can also receive a sparsity prior
\[
\|A_{:,c}\|_1
\]
which is useful when a component is expected to be compact rather than smooth. This is the mechanism currently used to test GC-like components against a smooth galaxy/background decomposition.

title: Model
text:
Optimization
The torch implementation follows a simple projected-gradient strategy:

Initialize (A) and (S) randomly with positive entries.
Optimize the loss with Adam.
Clamp (A) and (S) to remain non-negative after each step.
Return spectra, component weights, and the reconstruction (AS).

title: Model
text:
Sanity Checks
The current tests enforce two baseline conditions:

setting lambda_spatial = 0 recovers the original smooth NMF objective
adding sparse priors improves recovery of compact-source components on a synthetic IFU mock

See Getting Started for code examples and Benchmark for the current real-cube test.

title: Getting Started
text:
What the outputs mean

fit$spatial contains one component weight per spaxel and per component.
fit$spectra contains the recovered component spectra.
fit$reconstruction is the model approximation A %*% S.
fit$loss stores the optimization history.
fitted(fit, nx, ny) and predict(fit, type = "cube", nx, ny) reshape that reconstruction back into a cube.
residuals(fit, x = ...) returns data minus reconstruction.

title: Toy Benchmark
text:
This page isolates the base matrix factorization problem from the full IFU stress tests. The toy data are constructed to be exactly low-rank, with non-negative component spectra and non-negative spatial weights. Spatial and sparsity penalties are turned off for spax_nmf(), so this comparison checks the standalone vanilla NMF fit directly against NMF::nmf(). Under these conditions spax_nmf() still uses the torch-based Adam optimizer, with all regularization weights set to zero, so the comparison checks the actual package implementation against a standard NMF::nmf() reference.

If this toy benchmark behaves well while the real-cube benchmark does not, the core vanilla NMF machinery is likely fine and the remaining difficulty lies in the astrophysical data model rather than in the factorization code itself.

title: Toy Benchmark
text:
Interpretation
This toy benchmark should be read as a sanity check, not as a realistic IFU science case. The expected outcome is that both spax_nmf() and NMF::nmf() recover the low-rank structure well. If they do, then poor behavior on the real benchmark should be attributed to the harder galaxy+sky+ compact-source problem rather than to a basic failure of standalone NMF.
